---
title: "Choosing the Right Iterator"
---

# Choosing the Right Iterator

`Vec<T>` can produce three iterators. They differ in what you are allowed to do with `T` afterwards.

## The concept

| Method | Borrows the collection as | Yields | Collection afterwards |
|--------|---------------------------|--------|------------------------|
| `iter()` | `&self` | `&T` | Still fully usable |
| `iter_mut()` | `&mut self` | `&mut T` | Still usable, items may have changed |
| `into_iter()` | `self` | `T` | Moved. You cannot use it again |

`for x in collection` calls `IntoIterator::into_iter`. For a `Vec<T>` that moves the vector. For `&Vec<T>` it yields `&T`. For `&mut Vec<T>` it yields `&mut T`.

## Recipe 4 — Reading a collection without consuming it

```rust
fn main() {
    let readings = vec![18, 21, 19, 22];
    let hot: Vec<_> = readings.iter().copied().filter(|n| *n >= 21).collect();

    assert_eq!(hot, [21, 22]);
    assert_eq!(readings.iter().sum::<i32>(), 80);
}
```

`iter` yields `&i32`. `copied` turns that into `i32` because `i32` is `Copy`. The second `sum` is only legal because `readings` was not moved.

`copied` is the right call for `Copy` items. `cloned` is the call when you need an owned clone of something that is only `Clone`, such as `String`.

## Recipe 5 — Modifying elements in place

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut readings = vec![18, 21, 19];
    for slot in &mut readings {
        *slot += 1;
    }
    assert_eq!(readings, [19, 22, 20]);

    readings.iter_mut().for_each(|slot| *slot *= 2);
    assert_eq!(readings, [38, 44, 40]);
}
```

You cannot hold an `&mut` from `iter_mut` and also call `&self` methods on `readings` in the same breath. Finish the mutable iteration, then read.

## Recipe 6 — Consuming a collection to produce a new one

Use this when the old collection should not exist beside the new one. The elements move. No clone.

```rust
fn main() {
    let names = vec![String::from("ada"), String::from("linus")];
    let labels: Vec<String> = names.into_iter().map(|name| name.to_uppercase()).collect();

    assert_eq!(labels, ["ADA", "LINUS"]);
    // names is gone. Using it here would not compile.
}
```

If you still need the originals, go back to recipe 4 and clone only the values you keep.

## Recipe 7 — Understanding what for x in v actually does

This program shows the three forms side by side.

```rust
fn main() {
    let mut v = vec![String::from("a"), String::from("b")];

    let mut borrowed = Vec::new();
    for item in &v {
        borrowed.push(item.clone());
    }

    for item in &mut v {
        item.push('!');
    }

    let mut owned = Vec::new();
    for item in v {
        owned.push(item);
    }

    assert_eq!(borrowed, ["a", "b"]);
    assert_eq!(owned, ["a!", "b!"]);
}
```

The desugaring of `for item in iterable { body }` is:

```text
let mut iter = IntoIterator::into_iter(iterable);
loop {
    match iter.next() {
        Some(item) => { body }
        None => break,
    }
}
```

Which `into_iter` runs depends on the type of `iterable`:

- `v` is `Vec<String>`, so the vector moves and `item` is `String`.
- `&v` is `&Vec<String>`. Its `IntoIterator` yields `&String`.
- `&mut v` yields `&mut String`.

A common slip is writing `for item in v` when a later line still needs `v`. The compiler reports that `v` was moved. The fix is `for item in &v`, not a clone of the whole vector, unless you really need two owned copies.
